blocks.name: Numbers
blocks.blurb: Remainders, factorials, factors, HCF & LCM, progressions

questions.text: What is the remainder when 7<sup>103</sup> is divided by 25?
solution: 7<sup>2</sup> = 49 = 50 − 1, so 7<sup>2</sup> leaves remainder −1 when divided by 25.
questions.explanation: Look for a small power of the base that is 1 or −1 more or less than a multiple of the divisor. Once you have it, the huge power collapses to a small one. Option 7 is the remainder of 7<sup>1</sup>; 24 is what you get if you stop at 7<sup>2</sup> ≡ −1 and forget the leftover 7<sup>3</sup>.

questions.text: What is the highest power of 12 that divides 50! exactly?
solution: 12 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 3, so count the 2s and the 3s in 50!.
Each 12 needs two 2s, so the 2s allow ⌊47/2⌋ = 23 twelves.
questions.explanation: For a composite divisor, split it into prime powers, count each prime in n! with the ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p²⌋ + … rule, divide by the exponent, and take the minimum. 23 is the trap of checking only the 2s; 47 forgets that 12 needs two 2s; 16 counts only the multiples of 3 once.

questions.text: How many factors of 2160 are perfect squares?
solution: A perfect-square factor needs an even power of every prime.
Power of 2 can be 0, 2 or 4 (3 choices); power of 3 can be 0 or 2 (2 choices); power of 5 must be 0 (1 choice).
questions.explanation: Counting factors is always "choices for each exponent, multiplied". The square restriction just limits each exponent to even values. 8 comes from allowing 5<sup>1</sup>; 12 is the number of factors of 2<sup>4</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup>, which forgets the evenness rule on the 2s.

questions.text: Two positive numbers have HCF 12 and LCM 720. How many such pairs of numbers exist (order does not matter)?
solution: Write the numbers as 12a and 12b with a and b co-prime.
Because a and b are co-prime, each prime power (4, 3, 5) must go wholly to a or wholly to b.
Three prime powers can be split in 23 = 8 ordered ways, i.e. 8/2 = 4 unordered pairs: (1, 60), (4, 15), (3, 20), (5, 12).
questions.explanation: With HCF h and LCM l, the problem reduces to splitting l/h into two co-prime parts: 2<sup>k−1</sup> unordered ways for k distinct primes. The common slip is splitting 60 into any two factors, e.g. (2, 30) or (6, 10), which are not co-prime and would change the HCF.

questions.text: The sum of the first 20 terms of an arithmetic progression is 610 and the sum of the first 30 terms is 1365. What is its 40th term?
questions.explanation: Turning each sum into a "2a + (n − 1)d" equation gives two simple linear equations. Shortcut: S<sub>n</sub>/n is the average of the first n terms, which equals the term at position (n + 1)/2. So the 10.5th term is 30.5 and the 15.5th term is 45.5; 5 positions add 15, so d = 3. 122 and 116 are the 41st and 39th terms.

questions.text: The average of 11 results is 50. The average of the first six is 49 and the average of the last six is 52. What is the sixth result?
solution: First six total = 6 × 49 = 294; last six total = 6 × 52 = 312.
Adding the two groups counts the 6th result twice: 294 + 312 = 606.
questions.explanation: Whenever two groups overlap in exactly one item, (group 1 total + group 2 total − overall total) isolates that item. Deviation method: the first six are 6 below average in total and the last six are 12 above, so the shared result is 50 − 6 + 12 = 56.

questions.text: The average age of 30 students is 14 years. When the teacher’s age is included, the average rises by 1 year. How old is the teacher?
solution: With the teacher there are 31 people averaging 15: total = 465.
questions.explanation: Deviation shortcut: the teacher brings their own share of the new average (15) and also lifts each of the 30 students by 1. Teacher = 15 + 30 × 1 = 45. 44 uses 14 + 30; 31 forgets the teacher’s own share.

questions.text: Milk costs ₹40 per litre. How many litres of water must be added to 60 litres of milk so that the mixture is worth ₹32 per litre?
solution: Water costs nothing, so the value of the mixture is all from the milk: 60 × 40 = ₹2400.
At ₹32 per litre, ₹2400 buys 2400 ÷ 32 = 75 litres of mixture.
questions.explanation: Alligation view: milk at 40 and water at 0 mix to 32, so milk : water = (32 − 0) : (40 − 32) = 4 : 1. 60 litres of milk needs 15 of water. 12 comes from taking 20% of 60, but the price falls by 20% because water becomes 20% of the final mixture, not 20% of the milk.

questions.text: A vessel holds 80 litres of pure milk. 8 litres are taken out and replaced with water, and this is done three times in all. How much milk is left?
solution: Each replacement removes 8/80 = 1/10 of whatever milk is in the vessel, leaving 9/10 of it.
questions.explanation: Repeated replacement is compound decay: final = initial × (1 − removed/capacity)<sup>n</sup>. 56 litres assumes 8 litres of milk leaves every time (simple subtraction), which is wrong after the first round because later you remove a mixture. 64.8 litres is the answer after two rounds.

questions.text: Alloy A has gold and copper in the ratio 2 : 3, and alloy B has them in the ratio 7 : 3. In what ratio must A and B be melted together to get an alloy with gold and copper in the ratio 3 : 2?
solution: Work with the fraction of gold: A is 2/5 = 0.4, B is 7/10 = 0.7, and the target is 3/5 = 0.6.
Check: 1 kg of A and 2 kg of B give 0.4 + 1.4 = 1.8 kg of gold in 3 kg, i.e. 0.6.
questions.explanation: Alligation only works on the same kind of quantity, here the gold fraction of each alloy. Converting both ratios to “share of gold” is the key step. 2 : 1 is the classic slip of writing the differences the wrong way round: the alloy closer to the target needs the larger share.

blocks.name: Arithmetic
blocks.blurb: Percentages, profit & loss, interest, time & work, speed

questions.text: A earns 25% more than B, and B earns 20% less than C. How does A’s salary compare with C’s?
options: A and C earn the same
solution: Let C = 100. B is 20% less: B = 80.
A is 25% more than B: A = 80 × 1.25 = 100.
So A = C: they earn the same.
questions.explanation: A 20% fall is ×4/5 and a 25% rise is ×5/4; they cancel exactly. Remember the pair 20% ↔ 25%: a fall of 1/5 is undone by a rise of 1/4. The “5%” options come from adding and subtracting the percentages directly, which only works when they are applied to the same base.

questions.text: A trader marks goods 40% above cost and then allows two successive discounts of 10% each. What is the profit percentage?
questions.explanation: Successive changes multiply: 1.4 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 1.134. Two 10% discounts are a single 19% discount (10 + 10 − 10×10/100), not 20%. 20% subtracts the discounts from the markup; 12% treats the two discounts as 20% off and still subtracts wrongly.

questions.text: The difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on a sum for 2 years at 10% per annum is ₹150. What is the sum?
solution: For 2 years, CI − SI = P × (r/100)<sup>2</sup>: it is the interest earned on the first year’s interest.
questions.explanation: The only extra money under compound interest in year 2 is interest on year 1’s interest: P × r/100 × r/100. For 3 years the gap is P(r/100)<sup>2</sup>(3 + r/100). ₹1,500 multiplies by 10 instead of 100.

questions.text: A can finish a job in 12 days and B in 18 days. They work together for 4 days, and then A leaves. How many more days does B need to finish the job?
solution: Take the job as 36 units (LCM of 12 and 18). A does 3 units a day, B does 2.
Remaining = 36 − 20 = 16 units, which B does at 2 a day: 8 more days.
questions.explanation: Choosing total work as the LCM of the individual times makes every rate a whole number and avoids fractions. 6 days assumes B works at A’s rate; 10 days forgets that B also worked during the first 4 days.

questions.text: A train 240 m long passes a man walking at 6 km/h in the same direction in 16 seconds. What is the speed of the train?
solution: To pass the man, the train covers its own length, 240 m, at the relative speed.
Same direction, so relative speed = train − man: train = 54 + 6 = 60 km/h.
questions.explanation: Relative speed subtracts for same direction and adds for opposite directions. 54 km/h stops at the relative speed; 48 km/h subtracts the man’s speed instead of adding it back (that would be right only if they were moving towards each other); 66 km/h adds the man’s speed twice. Draw the directions before choosing + or −.

questions.text: A right triangle has legs of 20 cm and 21 cm. What is the radius of its inscribed circle?
solution: For a right triangle, inradius r = (a + b − c)/2 = (20 + 21 − 29)/2 = 6 cm.
Check with r = Area/s: area = 210, semi-perimeter s = 35, r = 6.
questions.explanation: 20-21-29 is a Pythagorean triplet worth remembering. The formula r = (a + b − c)/2 comes from the two tangents from each acute vertex. 14.5 cm is the circumradius (half the hypotenuse), the most common mix-up with the inradius.

questions.text: Two parallel chords of a circle of radius 17 cm have lengths 16 cm and 30 cm, and lie on opposite sides of the centre. How far apart are the chords?
solution: The perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord, so distance = √(r² − (half-chord)²).
16 cm chord: √(17² − 8²) = √225 = 15 cm from the centre.
30 cm chord: √(17² − 15²) = √64 = 8 cm from the centre.
Opposite sides of the centre, so the distances add: 15 + 8 = 23 cm.
questions.explanation: 8-15-17 is a triplet, which makes both distances whole numbers. If the chords were on the same side, the answer would be 15 − 8 = 7 cm, which is the trap option.

questions.text: A solid cone of base radius 6 cm and height 8 cm is melted and recast into solid spheres of radius 2 cm. How many spheres are made?
questions.explanation: Melting and recasting keeps volume the same. Write both volumes with π and cancel it. 27 forgets the 1/3 in the cone’s volume; 18 uses r² instead of r³ for the sphere.

questions.text: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 156°. How many diagonals does it have?
solution: Exterior angles of any polygon add to 360°, so n = 360 ÷ 24 = 15 sides.
questions.explanation: Always go through the exterior angle: it gives the number of sides in one division. 105 is ¹⁵C₂, which counts the sides as well as the diagonals.

questions.text: What is the area of the triangle formed by the lines y = x, y = −x and y = 6?
solution: y = x and y = −x meet at the origin.
Base = distance between (−6, 6) and (6, 6) = 12; height = 6 (distance of the base from the origin).
questions.explanation: Find the vertices first; with a horizontal base, area is just ½ × base × height. 18 uses a base of 6 (one side only); 72 forgets the ½.

questions.text: If α and β are the roots of x² − 7x + 10 = 0, what is α³ + β³?
solution: Sum of roots α + β = 7; product αβ = 10.
Check: the roots are 2 and 5, and 8 + 125 = 133.
questions.explanation: Express symmetric expressions through the sum and product of roots; you never need the roots themselves. 343 is just (α + β)³; 313 subtracts 3αβ but forgets the (α + β) factor; 203 is (α + β)(α² + β²), which misses the −αβ term in α² − αβ + β².

questions.text: How many integers x satisfy |x − 3| + |x + 2| ≤ 9?
solution: |x − 3| + |x + 2| is the total distance from x to 3 and to −2 on the number line.
For any x between −2 and 3 that total is exactly 5, which is ≤ 9: all of −2…3 work.
questions.explanation: Read |x − a| as distance. Between the two points the sum is constant (the gap, 5); outside, it grows by 2 for every unit you move away. With 9 − 5 = 4 to spare, you can move 2 units beyond each end. 6 counts only −2…3; 9 or 11 are off-by-one slips at the endpoints.

questions.text: Solve log₂(x − 1) + log₂(x + 1) = 3.
solution: Logs need positive arguments: x − 1 > 0, so x > 1. Reject −3.
questions.explanation: After solving any log equation, check that every original log argument is positive. x = −3 is the classic extraneous root; x = 9 comes from treating log₂ 8 as 9 instead of 3.

questions.text: If f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x² − 1, what is f(g(2)) − g(f(1))?
questions.explanation: Evaluate composite functions from the inside out. f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) are generally different. 15 has the subtraction reversed; 0 assumes the composition order does not matter.

questions.text: What is the maximum value of f(x) = min(x + 5, 11 − 2x) over all real x?
solution: x + 5 increases and 11 − 2x decreases, so their minimum is largest where the two are equal.
questions.explanation: The maximum of the minimum of a rising and a falling line is at their intersection: anywhere else, one of them is lower. 11 and 5 are each line’s value at x = 0, and 9 is a midpoint guess.

questions.text: In how many different ways can the letters of the word LETTER be arranged?
solution: LETTER has 6 letters: L, E, T, T, E, R. E and T each appear twice.
questions.explanation: Divide by the factorial of each repeat count, because swapping identical letters gives the same word. 720 ignores the repeats; 360 divides out only one of the two pairs.

questions.text: Six people sit around a round table. In how many ways can they sit if two particular people must not sit next to each other?
solution: Arrangements with the two together: treat them as one unit, so 5 units around the table = 4! = 24, times 2 for their internal order = 48.
questions.explanation: For “not together”, count all and subtract “together”. Circular arrangements fix one seat, which is why it is (n − 1)!. 48 is the together count; 120 is the total.

questions.text: Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum is a prime number?
questions.explanation: For two dice, the number of ways to get sum s is 6 − |s − 7|. 7/18 (14/36) usually misses one way for 5 or 11; 1/2 is a guess.

questions.text: How many solutions in positive integers does a + b + c = 10 have?
solution: Positive integers: give each of a, b, c one unit first, leaving 7 to distribute freely.
Non-negative solutions of x + y + z = 7 = ⁹C₂ = 36 (7 stars and 2 bars).
questions.explanation: Positive solutions of x₁ + … + x<sub>r</sub> = n number ⁿ⁻¹C<sub>r−1</sub>; non-negative ones number ⁿ⁺ʳ⁻¹C<sub>r−1</sub>. 66 = ¹²C₂ counts non-negative solutions (zeros allowed), which the question excludes.

questions.text: In a group of 60 people, 35 like tea, 30 like coffee and 12 like neither. How many like both?
solution: People who like at least one = 60 − 12 = 48.
questions.explanation: Always remove the “neither” group before using the union formula. 5 forgets the 12 who like neither (65 − 60).
